explanations.answer: Send him on his way back home
explanations.explanation: Jacob, Isaac's son, walks up to Laban and says, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” He's talking about going home, not setting up shop where he is. Jacob has a destination in mind, and the destination is not Laban's front porch.

explanations.answer: Give him a field of his own
explanations.explanation: Jacob never asks for a field here. What he asks is, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” Laban is Jacob's father-in-law, and he's the one hearing this request. Jacob has his eyes on home, not on a piece of land next door.

explanations.answer: Let him build a house nearby
explanations.explanation: Staying close by isn't what Jacob has in mind. He says, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” A house next door would be a very short trip for a man who wants to go home. Jacob is packing for distance.

I can see why you'd think it, but Jacob does the opposite. He tells Laban, “Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way.” His family is going with him. A man who leaves his wives and kids behind is not asking for them by name.

Right, he's bringing the whole family. Jacob says, “Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way.” He's asking for them by name, so they're coming. This is a family road trip, friend, and nobody is getting left at the rest stop.

Laban says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” Divination is a way of seeking hidden answers, and Laban says that's how he learned it. Whatever his method, he names the LORD's blessing and ties it straight to Jacob. That's Laban admitting Jacob is good for business.

Laban doesn't say anything about a warning. He says he learned by divination that the LORD has blessed him because of Jacob. A warning would make Laban want Jacob gone. This says the opposite, and it's exactly why he wants Jacob to stay.

Nothing in Laban's words is about a test. He says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” Laban sounds like a man who already read the results. And the results say Jacob stays.

Jacob says it plain: “you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over.” That's Jacob making his case to Laban. He doesn't leave it at that, though, because he goes on to ask when he can provide for his own household. I'd call that a strong opening argument.

Jacob really does say this to Laban. His words are, “you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over.” He's pointing to how much Laban's flocks have grown under his care. Then he asks when he can provide for his own household.

Jacob asks for “every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat.” He says, “These will be my wages.” He asks for the flock's less common colors and leaves the rest for Laban. That's his whole offer, and it comes with that one condition.
That one's flipped around. Jacob asks for the speckled or spotted sheep, the dark-colored lambs, and the spotted or speckled goats. Those are his wages. The plain ones stay with Laban.

Jacob doesn't ask for a fraction at all. He names kinds of animals: every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. He's picking by color, not by percentage. No calculator needed for this deal.

Jacob says “my honesty will testify for me” when Laban comes to check on his wages. He's saying the flocks will show it. Any goat of his that isn't speckled or spotted, or lamb that isn't dark-colored, would be considered stolen. Jacob is telling Laban to check his work, and I respect a man who invites an audit.

Jacob doesn't bring up patience here. He says “my honesty will testify for me” when Laban comes to check his wages. The flocks will tell the story. Patience may come in handy, but honesty is the word he used.

Kindness is a fine thing, but it's not what Jacob names. He says “my honesty will testify for me.” Any animal of his that doesn't match would be considered stolen. That's the honesty he's talking about.
Laban doesn't turn him down. He says, “Agreed.” Then he adds, “Let it be as you have said.” That's a yes with a bow on it, and Jacob has the deal.
Right, Laban takes the deal. He says, “Agreed,” and then, “Let it be as you have said.” No haggling, no counteroffer. I think that's a man who just wants to shake hands and move on.

Laban removes the spotted and dark-colored animals and places them “under the care of his sons.” That's Laban's own sons, not Jacob's. The animals Jacob asked for are now with someone else. I think that's a lot of effort for one afternoon.
The text says Laban placed the animals under the care of his sons. Those are Laban's own sons. Jacob's sons aren't the ones watching them. Laban handed them off to his own household.

Leah and Rachel are Jacob's wives, but they aren't who Laban picks. The text says he put the animals under the care of his sons. So the animals go to Laban's sons. Leah and Rachel aren't part of this handoff.

Jacob peels the bark and exposes “the white inner wood of the branches.” He takes fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees and strips them down. What shows underneath is white. That's the whole point of the peeling.
No sap in this verse. Jacob peels the bark, “exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” White is the color he's after. The sap isn't mentioned.
That's the opposite color. The text says Jacob peeled the bark, “exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” So it's white wood on display. Nothing dark about it.

Jacob sets the peeled branches “in the watering troughs in front of the flocks coming in to drink.” The troughs are where the flocks have to go for water. So every animal walks right past the branches. I think that's Jacob picking his spot with care.

The pens aren't where Jacob puts the branches. He sets them in the watering troughs, in front of the flocks coming in to drink. That's where the animals come for water. Pens are for sleeping, and troughs are where the traffic is.
Jacob doesn't scatter them around the open fields. The verse says he set the peeled branches “in the watering troughs.” The flocks come to drink there. That's where the branches go.

The text says the flocks “bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted.” Those are the kinds of animals Jacob asked for as his wages. The flocks mated in front of the branches, and this is what came out. Genesis tells us what happened and doesn't explain why.

It happened exactly like the verse says. The flocks “bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted.” Those are the very animals Jacob asked for as his wages. They weren't plain, and I think Jacob noticed.
Jacob does the opposite. The text says he “set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban's animals.” His animals have their own space. No mixing allowed.

Right, he keeps them apart. The text says Jacob “set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban's animals.” His flocks stay separate from Laban's. That's Jacob keeping his own animals easy to count.

The verse says, “if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” He only puts them out for the stronger females. The weaker ones don't get the branches. I think that's a man who knows exactly what he's doing.

Thirsty isn't the word. All the animals came to the troughs to drink, so thirsty would cover most of them. The verse says, “if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” Weak is the one that decides it.
The verse doesn't say young. It says, “if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” The text names weak animals here, and it doesn't mention age. Weak is what decides it.
It goes the other way around. The text says “the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob.” The stronger animals end up on Jacob's side of the ledger. Laban gets the weaker ones.

Right, the weaker ones go to Laban. The text says, “the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob.” So Jacob ends up with the stronger animals. I think Laban got the short end of that stick.

The text says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He owned large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. That's a long way from asking when he could provide for his own household. I think his accountant would've been smiling.

explanations.answer: He loses most of his flocks
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other way. It says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He ends up with large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. Nothing about losing his flocks.

Jacob doesn't end up in debt. The text says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He owned large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. That's a man with plenty, not a man with a tab.
